# Data location

Last updated Jun 26, 2026|Copy as Markdown|View as Markdown|Agent setup

[Select]

## Restrict Durable Objects to a jurisdiction

Jurisdictions are used to create Durable Objects that only run and store data within a region to comply with local regulations such as the GDPR ↗ or FedRAMP ↗.

Workers may still access Durable Objects constrained to a jurisdiction from anywhere in the world. The jurisdiction constraint only controls where the Durable Object itself runs and persists data. Consider using Regional Services to control the regions from which Cloudflare responds to requests.

Logging

A `DurableObjectId` will be logged outside of the specified jurisdiction for billing and debugging purposes.

Durable Objects can be restricted to a specific jurisdiction by creating a `DurableObjectNamespace` restricted to a jurisdiction. All Durable Object ID methods are valid on IDs within a namespace restricted to a jurisdiction.
    
    `const euSubnamespace = env.MY_DURABLE_OBJECT.jurisdiction("eu");
    const euId = euSubnamespace.newUniqueId();`

  * It is possible to have the same name represent different IDs in different jurisdictions.
    
    `const euId1 = env.MY_DURABLE_OBJECT.idFromName("my-name");
    const euId2 = env.MY_DURABLE_OBJECT.jurisdiction("eu").idFromName("my-name");
    console.assert(!euId1.equal(euId2), "This should always be true");`

  * You will run into an error if the jurisdiction on your `DurableObjectNamespace` and the jurisdiction on `DurableObjectId` are different.

  * You will not run into an error if the `DurableObjectNamespace` is not associated with a jurisdiction.

  * All Durable Object ID methods are valid on IDs within a namespace restricted to a jurisdiction.
    
    `const euSubnamespace = env.MY_DURABLE_OBJECT.jurisdiction("eu");
    const euId = euSubnamespace.idFromName(name);
    const stub = env.MY_DURABLE_OBJECT.get(euId);`

Use `DurableObjectNamespace.jurisdiction`

When specifying a jurisdiction, Cloudflare recommends you first create a namespace restricted to a jurisdiction, using `const euSubnamespace = env.MY_DURABLE_OBJECT.jurisdiction("eu")`.

Note that it is also possible to specify a jurisdiction by creating an individual `DurableObjectId` restricted to a jurisdiction, using `const euId = env.MY_DURABLE_OBJECT.newUniqueId({ jurisdiction: "eu" })`.

However, Cloudflare does not recommend this approach.

### Supported locations

Parameter  | Location
--- | ---
eu  | The European Union
us  | The United States
fedramp  | FedRAMP-Moderate data centers

### Read the jurisdiction from inside a Durable Object

The jurisdiction of a Durable Object is available inside the object via `ctx.id.jurisdiction`. The value is preserved across `toString()` and `idFromString()` round-trips and is also available inside alarm handlers for alarms scheduled on 2026-03-15 or later, which makes it suitable for region-aware logic inside the Durable Object.

## Provide a location hint

Durable Objects, as with any stateful API, will often add response latency as requests must be forwarded to the data center where the Durable Object, or state, is located.

Durable Objects do not currently change locations after they are created^{1}. By default, a Durable Object is instantiated in a data center close to where the initial `get()` request is made. This may not be in the same data center that the `get()` request is made from, but in most cases, it will be in close proximity.

Initial requests to Durable Objects

It can negatively impact latency to pre-create Durable Objects prior to the first client request or when the first client request is not representative of where the majority of requests will come from. It is better for latency to create Durable Objects in response to actual production traffic or provide explicit location hints.

Location hints are the mechanism provided to specify the location that a Durable Object should be located regardless of where the initial `get()` request comes from.

To manually create Durable Objects in another location, provide an optional `locationHint` parameter to `get()`. Only the first call to `get()` for a particular Object will respect the hint.
    
    `let durableObjectStub = OBJECT_NAMESPACE.get(id, { locationHint: "enam" });`

Caution

Hints are a best effort and not a guarantee. Unlike with jurisdictions, Durable Objects will not necessarily be instantiated in the hinted location, but instead instantiated in a data center selected to minimize latency from the hinted location.

### Supported locations

Parameter  | Location
--- | ---
wnam  | Western North America
enam  | Eastern North America
sam  | South America ^{2}
weur  | Western Europe
eeur  | Eastern Europe
apac  | Asia-Pacific
apac-ne  | Northeast Asia-Pacific ^{3}
apac-se  | Southeast Asia-Pacific ^{3}
oc  | Oceania
afr  | Africa ^{2}
me  | Middle East ^{2}

^{1} Dynamic relocation of existing Durable Objects is planned for the future.

^{2} Durable Objects currently do not spawn in this location. Instead, the Durable Object will spawn in a nearby location which does support Durable Objects. For example, Durable Objects hinted to South America spawn in Eastern North America instead.

^{3} `apac-ne` (Northeast Asia-Pacific) and `apac-se` (Southeast Asia-Pacific) are narrower sub-regions within `apac` (Asia-Pacific). Prefer `apac` for general Asia-Pacific placement. Choose `apac-ne` or `apac-se` only when your users are concentrated in the northeast or southeast of the region and you want to minimize latency for them.

# What are Durable Objects?

Last updated Jul 15, 2026|Copy as Markdown|View as Markdown|Agent setup

[Select]

A Durable Object is a special kind of Cloudflare Worker which uniquely combines compute with storage. Like a Worker, a Durable Object is automatically provisioned geographically close to where it is first requested, starts up quickly when needed, and shuts down when idle. You can have millions of them around the world. However, unlike regular Workers:

  * Each Durable Object has a globally-unique name, which allows you to send requests to a specific object from anywhere in the world. Thus, a Durable Object can be used to coordinate between multiple clients who need to work together.
  * Each Durable Object has some durable storage attached. Since this storage lives together with the object, it is strongly consistent yet fast to access.

Therefore, Durable Objects enable stateful serverless applications.

## Durable Objects highlights

Durable Objects have properties that make them a great fit for distributed stateful scalable applications.

Serverless compute, zero infrastructure management

  * Durable Objects are built on-top of the Workers runtime, so they support exactly the same code (JavaScript and WASM), and similar memory and CPU limits.
  * Each Durable Object is implicitly created on first access. User applications are not concerned with their lifecycle, creating them or destroying them. Durable Objects migrate among healthy servers, and therefore applications never have to worry about managing them.
  * Each Durable Object stays alive as long as requests are being processed, and remains alive for several seconds after being idle before hibernating, allowing applications to exploit in-memory caching while handling many consecutive requests and boosting their performance.

Storage colocated with compute

  * Each Durable Object has its own durable, transactional, and strongly consistent storage (up to 10 GB^{1}), persisted across requests, and accessible only within that object.

Single-threaded concurrency

  * Each Durable Object instance has an identifier, either randomly-generated or user-generated, which allows you to globally address which Durable Object should handle a specific action or request.
  * Durable Objects are single-threaded and cooperatively multi-tasked, just like code running in a web browser. For more details on how safety and correctness are achieved, refer to the blog post "Durable Objects: Easy, Fast, Correct — Choose three" ↗.

Elastic horizontal scaling across Cloudflare's global network

  * Durable Objects can be spread around the world, and you can optionally influence where each instance should be located. Durable Objects are not yet available in every Cloudflare data center; refer to the where.durableobjects.live ↗ project for live locations.
  * Each Durable Object type (or "Namespace binding" in Cloudflare terms) corresponds to a JavaScript class implementing the actual logic. 
## Actor programming model

Another way to describe and think about Durable Objects is through the lens of the Actor programming model ↗. There are several popular examples of the Actor model supported at the programming language level through runtimes or library frameworks, like Erlang ↗, Elixir ↗, Akka ↗, or Microsoft Orleans for .NET ↗.

The Actor model simplifies a lot of problems in distributed systems by abstracting away the communication between actors using RPC calls (or message sending) that could be implemented on-top of any transport protocol, and it avoids most of the concurrency pitfalls you get when doing concurrency through shared memory such as race conditions when multiple processes/threads access the same data in-memory.

Each Durable Object instance can be seen as an Actor instance, receiving messages (incoming HTTP/RPC requests), executing some logic in its own single-threaded context using its attached durable storage or in-memory state, and finally sending messages to the outside world (outgoing HTTP/RPC requests or responses), even to another Durable Object instance.

# Known issues

Last updated Jul 3, 2026|Copy as Markdown|View as Markdown|Agent setup

[Select]

Durable Objects is generally available. However, there are some known issues.

## Global uniqueness

Global uniqueness guarantees there is only a single instance of a Durable Object class with a given ID running at once, across the world.

Uniqueness is enforced upon starting a new event (such as receiving an HTTP request), and upon accessing storage.

After an event is received, if the event takes some time to execute and does not ever access its durable storage, then it is possible that the Durable Object may no longer be current, and some other instance of the same Durable Object ID will have been created elsewhere. If the event accesses storage at this point, it will receive an exception. If the event completes without ever accessing storage, it may not ever realize that the Durable Object was no longer current.

A Durable Object may be replaced in the event of a network partition or a software update (including either an update of the Durable Object's class code, or of the Workers system itself). Enabling `wrangler tail` or Cloudflare dashboard ↗ logs requires a software update.

## Code updates

Code changes for Workers and Durable Objects are released globally in an eventually consistent manner. Because each Durable Object is globally unique, the situation can arise that a request arrives to the latest version of your Worker (running in one part of the world), which then calls to a unique Durable Object running the previous version of your code for a short period of time (typically seconds to minutes). If you create a gradual deployment, this period of time is determined by how long your live deployment is configured to use more than one version.

For this reason, it is best practice to ensure that API changes between your Workers and Durable Objects are forward and backward compatible across code updates.

## New `us` jurisdiction for Durable Objects

Durable ObjectsWorkers

Durable Objects now supports a `us` jurisdiction, letting you create Durable Objects that only run and store data within the United States. Use the `us` jurisdiction when you need to keep a Durable Object's compute and storage inside the United States to meet data residency requirements.

Create a namespace restricted to the `us` jurisdiction the same way as any other jurisdiction:
    
    `// Worker
    export default {
    	async fetch(request, env) {
    		const usSubnamespace = env.MY_DURABLE_OBJECT.jurisdiction("us");
    		const stub = usSubnamespace.getByName("general");
    		return stub.fetch(request);
    	},
    };`

Workers may still access Durable Objects constrained to the `us` jurisdiction from anywhere in the world. The jurisdiction constraint only controls where the Durable Object itself runs and persists data.

For the full list of supported jurisdictions, refer to Data location — Restrict Durable Objects to a jurisdiction.

# Service bindings

Last updated Aug 18, 2026|Copy as Markdown|View as Markdown|Agent setup

## About Service bindings

Service bindings allow one Worker to call into another, without going through a publicly-accessible URL. A Service binding allows Worker A to call a method on Worker B, or to forward a request from Worker A to Worker B.

Service bindings provide the separation of concerns that microservice or service-oriented architectures provide, without configuration pain, performance overhead or need to learn RPC protocols.

  * Service bindings are fast. When you use Service Bindings, there is zero overhead or added latency. By default, both Workers run on the same thread of the same Cloudflare server. And when you enable Smart Placement, each Worker runs in the optimal location for overall performance.
  * Service bindings are not just HTTP. Worker A can expose methods that can be directly called by Worker B. Communicating between services only requires writing JavaScript methods and classes.

For example, if you want Worker A to be able to call Worker B — you'd add the following to the Wrangler configuration file for Worker A:
    
    `{
    	"services": [
    		{
    			"binding": "<BINDING_NAME>",
    			"service": "<WORKER_NAME>"
    		}
    	]
    }`
    
    `[[services]]
    binding = "<BINDING_NAME>"
    service = "<WORKER_NAME>"`

  * `binding`: The name of the key you want to expose on the `env` object.
  * `service`: The name of the target Worker you would like to communicate with. This Worker must be on your Cloudflare account.

## Interfaces

Worker A that declares a Service binding to Worker B can call Worker B in two different ways:

  1. RPC lets you communicate between Workers using function calls that you define. For example, `await env.BINDING_NAME.myMethod(arg1)`. This is recommended for most use cases, and allows you to create your own internal APIs that your Worker makes available to other Workers.
  2. HTTP lets you communicate between Workers by calling the `fetch()` handler from other Workers, sending `Request` objects and receiving `Response` objects back. For example, `env.BINDING_NAME.fetch(request)`.

Cloudflare Access context

Cloudflare Access does not propagate `ctx.access` from Worker A to Worker B. This applies to HTTP requests and RPC invocations. Do not treat the downstream invocation as authenticated by the caller's Access context. For more information, refer to `ctx.access` limitations.

    	"name": "worker_b",
    	"main": "./src/workerB.js"
    }`
    
    `"$schema" = "./node_modules/wrangler/config-schema.json"
    name = "worker_b"
    main = "./src/workerB.js"`
    
    `import { WorkerEntrypoint } from "cloudflare:workers";
    
    export default class WorkerB extends WorkerEntrypoint {

When making changes to existing Workers, in most cases you should:

  * Deploy changes to Worker B first, in a way that is compatible with the existing Worker A. For example, add a new method to Worker B.
  * Next, deploy changes to Worker A. For example, call the new method on Worker B, from Worker A.
  * Finally, remove any unused code. For example, delete the previously used method on Worker B.

## Smart Placement

Smart Placement automatically places your Worker in an optimal location that minimizes latency.

You can use Smart Placement together with Service bindings to split your Worker into two services:

Image: Smart Placement and Service Bindings

Refer to the docs on Smart Placement for more.

## Limits

Service bindings have the following limits:

  * Each request to a Worker via a Service binding counts toward your subrequest limit.
  * A single request has a maximum of 32 Worker invocations, and each call to a Service binding counts towards this limit. Subsequent calls will throw an exception.
  * Calling a service binding does not count towards simultaneous open connection limits

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much work can a single Durable Object do?

Durable Objects can scale horizontally across many Durable Objects. Each individual Object is inherently single-threaded.

  * An individual Object has a soft limit of 1,000 requests per second. You can have an unlimited number of individual objects per namespace.
  * A simple storage `get()` on a small value that directly returns the response may realize a higher request throughput compared to a Durable Object that (for example) serializes and/or deserializes large JSON values.
  * Similarly, a Durable Object that performs multiple `list()` operations may be more limited in terms of request throughput.

A Durable Object that receives too many requests will, after attempting to queue them, return an overloaded error to the caller.

### How many Durable Objects can I create?

Durable Objects are designed such that the number of individual objects in the system do not need to be limited, and can scale horizontally.

# Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

In Default mode, strongly prefer making reasonable assumptions and executing the user's request rather than stopping to ask questions. If you absolutely must ask a question because the answer cannot be discovered from local context and a reasonable assumption would be risky, ask the user directly with a concise plain-text question. Never write a multiple choice question as a textual assistant message.

L561: # Placement
L562: 
L563: Last updated Apr 23, 2026|Copy as Markdown|cite378†View as Markdown |cite369†Agent setup L564: 
L565: [Select]
L566: By default, cite1†Workers and cite379†Pages Functions run in a data center closest to where the request was received. If your Worker makes requests to back-end infrastructure such as databases or APIs, it may be more performant to run that Worker closer to your back-end than the end user.
L567: 
L568:     `{
L569:     	"placement": {
L570:     		// Use one of the following options (mutually exclusive):
L571:     		"mode": "smart", // Cloudflare automatically places your Worker closest to the upstream with the most requests
L572:     		"region": "gcp:us-east4", // Explicit cloud region to run your Worker closest to - e.g. "gcp:us-east4" or "aws:us-east-1"
L573:     		"host": "db.example.com:5432", // A host to probe (TCP/layer 4) - e.g. a database host - and place your Worker closest to
L574:     		"hostname": "api.example.com", // A hostname to probe (HTTP/layer 7) - e.g. an API endpoint - and place your Worker closest to
L575:     	},
L576:     }`
L577: 
L578:     `[placement]
L579:     mode = "smart"
L580:     region = "gcp:us-east4"
L581:     host = "db.example.com:5432"
L582:     hostname = "api.example.com"`
L583: Placement can reduce the overall latency of a Worker request by minimizing roundtrip latency of requests between your Worker and back-end services. You can achieve single-digit millisecond latency to databases, APIs, and other services running in legacy cloud infrastructure.
L584: Option  | Best for  | Configuration
L585: --- | --- | ---
L586: Smart  | Multiple back-end services, or unknown infrastructure locations  | `mode = "smart"`
L587: Region  | Single back-end service in a known cloud region  | `region`
L588: Host  | Single back-end service not in a major cloud provider  | `host` or `hostname`
L589: ## Understand placement
L590: 
L591: Consider a user in Sydney, Australia accessing an application running on Workers. This application makes multiple round trips to a database in Frankfurt, Germany.
L592: 
L593: cite380†Image: A user located in Sydney, AU connecting to a Worker in the same region which then makes multiple round trips to a database located in Frankfurt, DE.  L594: The latency from multiple round trips between Sydney and Frankfurt adds up. By placing the Worker near the database, Cloudflare reduces the total request duration.
L595: 
L596: cite381†Image: A user located in Sydney, AU connecting to a Worker in Frankfurt, DE which then makes multiple round trips to a database also located in Frankfurt, DE.  L597: ## Enable Smart Placement
L598: 
L599: Smart Placement automatically analyzes your Worker's traffic patterns and places it in an optimal location. Use Smart Placement when:
L600: 
L601:   * Your Worker connects to multiple back-end services
L602:   * You do not know the exact location of your infrastructure
L603:   * Your back-end services are distributed or replicated
L604: 
L605: Smart Placement is enabled on a per-Worker basis. Once enabled, it analyzes the cite382†request duration of the Worker in different Cloudflare locations on a regular basis.
L606: For each candidate location, Smart Placement considers the Worker's performance and the network latency added by forwarding the request. If a candidate location is significantly faster, the request is forwarded there. Otherwise, the Worker runs in the default location closest to the request.
L607: 
L608: Smart Placement only considers locations where the Worker has previously run. It cannot place your Worker in a location that does not normally receive traffic.
L609: ### Review limitations
L610: 
L611:   * Smart Placement only affects the execution of cite122†fetch event handlers . It does not affect cite81†RPC methods or cite383†named entrypoints .
L612:   * Workers without a fetch event handler are ignored by Smart Placement.
L613:   * cite166†Static assets are always served from the location nearest to the incoming request. If your code retrieves assets via the cite91†static assets binding , assets are served from the location where your Worker runs.
L614: ### Enable smart placement
L615: 
L616: Smart Placement is available on all Workers plans.
L617: 
L618: #### Configure with Wrangler
L619: 
L620: Add the following to your Wrangler configuration file:
L621: 
L622:     `{
L623:     	"placement": {
L624:     		"mode": "smart",
L625:     	},
L626:     }`
L627: 
L628:     `[placement]
L629:     mode = "smart"`
L630: 
L631: Smart Placement may take up to 15 minutes to analyze your Worker after deployment.
L632: #### Configure in the dashboard
L633: 
L634:   1. Go to Workers & Pages.
L635: 
L636: cite384†Go to Workers & Pages ↗†dash.cloudflare.com L637:   2. Select your Worker.
L638: 
L639:   3. Go to Settings > General.
L640: 
L641:   4. Under Placement, select Smart.
L642: 
L643: Smart Placement requires consistent traffic to the Worker from multiple locations to make a placement decision. The analysis process may take up to 15 minutes.
L644: ### Check placement status
L645: 
L646: Query your Worker's placement status through the Workers API:
L647: 
L648:     `curl -X GET https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$ACCOUNT_ID/workers/services/$WORKER_NAME \
L649:     -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN" \
L650:     -H "Content-Type: application/json" | jq .`
L651: 
L652: Possible placement states:
L653: Status  | Description
L654: --- | ---
L655: (not present)  | The Worker has not been analyzed yet. It runs in the default location closest to the request.
L656: `SUCCESS`  | The Worker was analyzed and will be optimized by Smart Placement.
L657: `INSUFFICIENT_INVOCATIONS`  | The Worker has not received enough requests from multiple locations to make a placement decision.
L658: `UNSUPPORTED_APPLICATION`  | Smart Placement made the Worker slower and reverted the placement. This state is rare (fewer than 1% of Workers).
L659: ### Review request duration analytics
L660: 
L661: Once Smart Placement is enabled, data about request duration is collected. Request duration is measured at the data center closest to the end user. By default, 1% of requests are not routed with Smart Placement to serve as a baseline for comparison.
L662: 
L663: View your Worker's cite382†request duration analytics to measure the impact of Smart Placement.
L664: ### Check the `cf-placement` header
L665: 
L666: Cloudflare adds a `cf-placement` header to all requests when placement is enabled. Use this header to check whether a request was routed with Smart Placement and where the Worker processed the request.
L667: 
L668: The header value includes a placement type and an airport code indicating the data center location:
L669:   * `remote-LHR` — The request was routed using Smart Placement to a data center near London.
L670:   * `local-EWR` — The request was not routed using Smart Placement. The Worker ran in the default location near Newark.
L671: 
L672: Caution
L673: 
L674: The `cf-placement` header may be removed before Smart Placement exits beta.
L675: ## Configure explicit Placement Hints
L676: 
L677: Placement Hints let you explicitly specify where your Worker runs. Use Placement Hints when:
L678: 
L679:   * You know the exact location of your back-end infrastructure
L680:   * Your Worker connects to a single database, API, or service
L681:   * Your infrastructure is single-homed (not replicated or anycasted)
L682: Examples include a primary database, a virtual machine, or a Kubernetes cluster in a specific region. Reducing round-trip latency from 20 to 30 milliseconds per query to 1 to 3 milliseconds improves response times.
L683: 
L684: Note
L685: Workers run on cite385†Cloudflare's global network ↗†www.cloudflare.com , not inside cloud provider regions. Placement Hints run your Worker in the data center with the lowest latency to your specified cloud region. At extremely high request volumes (hundreds of thousands of requests per second or more), Cloudflare may run instances across a more distributed area to balance traffic.

L565: # Service bindings
L566: 
L567: Last updated Aug 18, 2026|Copy as Markdown|cite378†View as Markdown |cite369†Agent setup L568:

L570: ## About Service bindings
L571: 
L572: Service bindings allow one Worker to call into another, without going through a publicly-accessible URL. A Service binding allows Worker A to call a method on Worker B, or to forward a request from Worker A to Worker B.
L573: 
L574: Service bindings provide the separation of concerns that microservice or service-oriented architectures provide, without configuration pain, performance overhead or need to learn RPC protocols.
L575:   * Service bindings are fast. When you use Service Bindings, there is zero overhead or added latency. By default, both Workers run on the same thread of the same Cloudflare server. And when you enable cite38†Smart Placement , each Worker runs in the optimal location for overall performance.
L576:   * Service bindings are not just HTTP. Worker A can expose methods that can be directly called by Worker B. Communicating between services only requires writing JavaScript methods and classes.
L577:   * Service bindings don't increase costs. You can split apart functionality into multiple Workers, without incurring additional costs. Learn more about cite379†pricing for Service Bindings .
L578: cite380†Image: Service bindings are a zero-cost abstraction L579: Service bindings are commonly used to:
L580:   * Provide a shared internal service to multiple Workers. For example, you can deploy an authentication service as its own Worker, and then have any number of separate Workers communicate with it via Service bindings.
L581:   * Isolate services from the public Internet. You can deploy a Worker that is not reachable via the public Internet, and can only be reached via an explicit Service binding that another Worker declares.
L582:   * Allow teams to deploy code independently. Team A can deploy their Worker on their own release schedule, and Team B can deploy their Worker separately.
L583: ## Configuration
L584: 
L585: You add a Service binding by modifying the cite319†Wrangler configuration file of the caller — the Worker that you want to be able to initiate requests.
L586: For example, if you want Worker A to be able to call Worker B — you'd add the following to the cite319†Wrangler configuration file for Worker A:
L587: 
L588:     `{
L589:     	"services": [
L590:     		{
L591:     			"binding": "<BINDING_NAME>",
L592:     			"service": "<WORKER_NAME>"
L593:     		}
L594:     	]
L595:     }`
L596: 
L597:     `[[services]]
L598:     binding = "<BINDING_NAME>"
L599:     service = "<WORKER_NAME>"`
L600:   * `binding`: The name of the key you want to expose on the `env` object.
L601:   * `service`: The name of the target Worker you would like to communicate with. This Worker must be on your Cloudflare account.
L602: ## Interfaces
L603: 
L604: Worker A that declares a Service binding to Worker B can call Worker B in two different ways:
L605:   1. cite381†RPC lets you communicate between Workers using function calls that you define. For example, `await env.BINDING_NAME.myMethod(arg1)`. This is recommended for most use cases, and allows you to create your own internal APIs that your Worker makes available to other Workers.
L606:   2. cite382†HTTP lets you communicate between Workers by calling the cite383†`fetch()` handler from other Workers, sending `Request` objects and receiving `Response` objects back. For example, `env.BINDING_NAME.fetch(request)`.
L607: Cloudflare Access context
L608: 
L609: Cloudflare Access does not propagate `ctx.access` from Worker A to Worker B. This applies to HTTP requests and RPC invocations. Do not treat the downstream invocation as authenticated by the caller's Access context. For more information, refer to cite384†`ctx.access` limitations .
L611: This example cite385†extends the `WorkerEntrypoint` class to support RPC-based Service bindings. First, create the Worker that you want to communicate with. Let's call this "Worker B". Worker B exposes the public method, `add(a, b)`:
L612: 
L613:     `{
L614:     	"$schema": "./node_modules/wrangler/config-schema.json",
L615:     	"name": "worker_b",
L616:     	"main": "./src/workerB.js"
L617:     }`
L618: 
L619:     `"$schema" = "./node_modules/wrangler/config-schema.json"
L620:     name = "worker_b"
L621:     main = "./src/workerB.js"`
L634: Next, create the Worker that will call Worker B. Let's call this "Worker A". Worker A declares a binding to Worker B. This is what gives it permission to call public methods on Worker B.
L635: 
L636:     `{
L637:     	"$schema": "./node_modules/wrangler/config-schema.json",
L638:     	"name": "worker_a",
L639:     	"main": "./src/workerA.js",
L640:     	"services": [
L641:     		{
L642:     			"binding": "WORKER_B",
L643:     			"service": "worker_b"
L644:     		}
L645:     	]
L646:     }`
L647: 
L648:     `"$schema" = "./node_modules/wrangler/config-schema.json"
L665: ## Lifecycle
L666: 
L667: The Service bindings API is asynchronous — you must `await` any method you call. If Worker A invokes Worker B via a Service binding, and Worker A does not await the completion of Worker B, Worker B will be terminated early.
L668: 
L669: For more about the lifecycle of calling a Worker over a Service Binding via RPC, refer to the cite388†RPC Lifecycle docs.
L671: Local development is supported for Service bindings. For each Worker, open a new terminal and use cite389†`wrangler dev` in the relevant directory. When running `wrangler dev`, service bindings will show as `connected`/`not connected` depending on whether Wrangler can find a running `wrangler dev` session for that Worker. For example:
L672: 
L673:     `$ wrangler dev
L674:     ...
L675:     Your worker has access to the following bindings:
L676:     - Services:
L677:       - SOME_OTHER_WORKER: some-other-worker [connected]
L678:       - ANOTHER_WORKER: another-worker [not connected]`
L683: ## Deployment
L684: 
L685: Workers using Service bindings are deployed separately.
L686: 
L687: When getting started and deploying for the first time, this means that the target Worker (Worker B in the examples above) must be deployed first, before Worker A. Otherwise, when you attempt to deploy Worker A, deployment will fail, because Worker A declares a binding to Worker B, which does not yet exist.
L688:

L693: ## Smart Placement
L694: 
L695: cite38†Smart Placement automatically places your Worker in an optimal location that minimizes latency.
L696: 
L697: You can use Smart Placement together with Service bindings to split your Worker into two services:
L698: 
L699: cite391†Image: Smart Placement and Service Bindings L700: 
L701: Refer to the cite392†docs on Smart Placement for more.
L702: ## Limits
L703: 
L704: Service bindings have the following limits:
L705: 
L706:   * Each request to a Worker via a Service binding counts toward your cite393†subrequest limit .
L707:   * A single request has a maximum of 32 Worker invocations, and each call to a Service binding counts towards this limit. Subsequent calls will throw an exception.
L708:   * Calling a service binding does not count towards cite394†simultaneous open connection limits L709:

L131: # Data location
L132:

L137: Learn how the location of data stored in R2 is determined and about the different available inputs that control the physical location where objects in your buckets are stored.
L138: ## Automatic (recommended)
L139: 
L140: When you create a new bucket, the data location is set to Automatic by default. Currently, this option chooses a bucket location in the closest available region to the create bucket request based on the location of the caller.
L141: ## Location Hints
L142: 
L143: Location Hints are optional parameters you can provide during bucket creation to indicate the primary geographical location you expect data will be accessed from.
L144: Using Location Hints can be a good choice when you expect the majority of access to data in a bucket to come from a different location than where the create bucket request originates. Keep in mind Location Hints are a best effort and not a guarantee, and they should only be used as a way to optimize performance by placing regularly updated content closer to users.
L145: ### Set hints via the Cloudflare dashboard
L146: 
L147: You can choose to automatically create your bucket in the closest available region based on your location or choose a specific location from the list.
L148: 
L149:   1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to the R2 object storage page.
L150: 
L151: cite87†Go to Overview ↗†dash.cloudflare.com L152:   2. Select Create bucket.
L153: 
L154:   3. Enter a name for the bucket.
L155: 
L156:   4. Under Location, leave None selected for automatic selection or choose a region from the list.
L157:   5. Select Create bucket to complete the bucket creation process.
L158: ### Set hints via the S3 API
L159: 
L160: You can set the Location Hint via the `LocationConstraint` parameter using the S3 API:
L161: 
L162:     `await S3.send(
L163:     	new CreateBucketCommand({
L164:     		Bucket: "YOUR_BUCKET_NAME",
L165:     		CreateBucketConfiguration: {
L166:     			LocationConstraint: "WNAM",
L167:     		},
L168:     	}),
L169:     );`
L170: 
L171: Refer to cite35†Examples for additional examples from other S3 SDKs.
L172: ### Available hints
L173: 
L174: The following hint locations are supported:
L175: 
L176: Hint  | Hint description
L177: --- | ---
L178: wnam  | Western North America
L179: enam  | Eastern North America
L180: weur  | Western Europe
L181: eeur  | Eastern Europe
L182: apac  | Asia-Pacific
L183: oc  | Oceania
L184: 
L185: ### Additional considerations
L186: 
L187: Location Hints are only honored the first time a bucket with a given name is created. If you delete and recreate a bucket with the same name, the original bucket’s location will be used.
L188: ## Jurisdictional Restrictions
L189: 
L190: Jurisdictional Restrictions guarantee objects in a bucket are stored within a specific jurisdiction.
L191: 
L192: Use Jurisdictional Restrictions when you need to ensure data is stored and processed within a jurisdiction to meet data residency requirements, including local regulations such as the cite88†GDPR ↗†gdpr-info.eu or cite89†FedRAMP ↗†blog.cloudflare.com .
L193: ### Set jurisdiction via the Cloudflare dashboard
L194: 
L195:   1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to the R2 object storage page.
L196: 
L197: cite87†Go to Overview ↗†dash.cloudflare.com L198:   2. Select Create bucket.
L199: 
L200:   3. Enter a name for the bucket.
L201: 
L202:   4. Under Location, select Specify jurisdiction and choose a jurisdiction from the list.
L203: 
L204:   5. Select Create bucket to complete the bucket creation process.
L205: ### Using jurisdictions from Workers
L206: To access R2 buckets that belong to a jurisdiction from cite90†Workers , you will need to specify the jurisdiction as well as the bucket name as part of your cite91†bindings in your cite92†Wrangler configuration file :
L207: 
L208:     `{
L209:     	"r2_buckets": [
L210:     		{
L211:     			"binding": "MY_BUCKET",
L212:     			"bucket_name": "<YOUR_BUCKET_NAME>",
L213:     			"jurisdiction": "<JURISDICTION>"
L214:     		}
L215:     	]
L216:     }`
L217: 
L218:     `[[r2_buckets]]
L219:     binding = "MY_BUCKET"
L220:     bucket_name = "<YOUR_BUCKET_NAME>"

L194: 
L195:   1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to the R2 object storage page.
L196: 
L197: cite87†Go to Overview ↗†dash.cloudflare.com L198:   2. Select Create bucket.
L199:

L201: 
L202:   4. Under Location, select Specify jurisdiction and choose a jurisdiction from the list.
L203: 
L204:   5. Select Create bucket to complete the bucket creation process.
L205: ### Using jurisdictions from Workers
L206: To access R2 buckets that belong to a jurisdiction from cite90†Workers , you will need to specify the jurisdiction as well as the bucket name as part of your cite91†bindings in your cite92†Wrangler configuration file :
L207: 
L208:     `{
L209:     	"r2_buckets": [
L210:     		{
L211:     			"binding": "MY_BUCKET",
L212:     			"bucket_name": "<YOUR_BUCKET_NAME>",
L213:     			"jurisdiction": "<JURISDICTION>"
L214:     		}
L215:     	]
L216:     }`

L221:     jurisdiction = "<JURISDICTION>"`
L222: For more information on getting started, refer to cite27†Use R2 from Workers .
L223: ### Using jurisdictions with the S3 API
L224: 
L225: When interacting with R2 resources that belong to a defined jurisdiction with the S3 API or existing S3-compatible SDKs, you must specify the cite93†jurisdiction in your S3 endpoint:
L226: 
L227: `https://<ACCOUNT_ID>.<JURISDICTION>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com`
L228: 
L229: You can use your jurisdiction-specific endpoint for any cite30†supported S3 API operations . When using a jurisdiction endpoint, you will not be able to access R2 resources outside of that jurisdiction.
L230: The example below shows how to create an R2 bucket in the `eu` jurisdiction using the cite94†`@aws-sdk/client-s3` ↗†www.npmjs.com package for JavaScript.
L231: 
L232:     `import { S3Client, CreateBucketCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
L233:     const S3 = new S3Client({
L234:     	endpoint: "https://<account_id>.eu.r2.cloudflarestorage.com",
L235:     	credentials: {
L236:     		accessKeyId: "<access_key_id>",
L237:     		secretAccessKey: "<access_key_secret>",
L238:     	},
L239:     	region: "auto",
L240:     });
L241:     await S3.send(
L242:     	new CreateBucketCommand({
L243:     		Bucket: "YOUR_BUCKET_NAME",
L244:     	}),
L245:     );`
L246: Refer to cite35†Examples for additional examples from other S3 SDKs.
L247: ### Available jurisdictions
L248: 
L249: The following jurisdictions are supported:
L250: 
L251: Jurisdiction  | Jurisdiction description
L252: --- | ---
L253: eu  | European Union
L254: fedramp  | FedRAMP
L255: us  | United States
L256: 
L257: Note
L258: 
L259: Cloudflare Enterprise customers may contact their account team or cite95†Cloudflare Support to get access to the FedRAMP jurisdiction.
L260: ### Limitations
L261: 
L262: The following services do not interact with R2 resources with assigned jurisdictions:
L263: 
L264:   * cite96†Logpush . As a workaround to this limitation, you can set up a cite97†Logpush job using an S3-compatible endpoint to store logs in an R2 bucket in the jurisdiction of your choice.

L123: ### Does Hyperdrive support connecting to D1 databases?
L124: 
L125: Hyperdrive does not support cite66†D1 because D1 provides fast connectivity from Workers by design.
L126: Hyperdrive is designed to speed up connectivity to traditional, regional SQL databases such as PostgreSQL. These databases are typically accessed using database drivers that communicate over TCP/IP. Unlike D1, creating a secure database connection to a traditional SQL database involves multiple round trips between the client (your Worker) and your database server. See cite4†How Hyperdrive works for more detail on why round trips are needed and how Hyperdrive solves this.
L127: D1 does not require round trips to create database connections. D1 is designed to be performant for access from Workers by default, without needing Hyperdrive.
L128: ### Should I use Placement with Hyperdrive?
L129: 
L130: Yes, if your Worker makes multiple queries per request. cite67†Placement runs your Worker near your database, reducing per-query latency from 20-30ms to 1-3ms. Hyperdrive handles connection pooling and setup. Placement reduces the network distance for query execution.
L131: 
L132: Use `placement.region` if your database runs in AWS, GCP, or Azure. Use `placement.host` for databases hosted elsewhere.
L133: 
L134: ## Caching
L135: ### Does Hyperdrive invalidate cached reads when I write to my database
L136: 
L137: No. Hyperdrive does not invalidate cached read query results when your application writes to your database. A matching read can return a cached result until the configured `max_age` expires, and Hyperdrive can serve that result during the `stale_while_revalidate` window while it refreshes the cache.
L138: Use a cache-disabled Hyperdrive configuration for reads that must return fresh data, such as authentication, sessions, permissions, or reads immediately after a write. Refer to cite68†Query caching to choose a caching strategy.
L139: ### Can I use Hyperdrive if some reads need read-after-write consistency
L140: 
L141: Yes. Configure two Hyperdrive bindings to the same database: one with query caching enabled for reads that can tolerate short staleness, and one with query caching disabled for reads that must be fresh. The cache-disabled binding still gives you Hyperdrive's connection pooling and fast connection setup.
L142: If an object-relational mapping (ORM) library or authentication library owns the SQL, create separate database clients for each binding and pass the cache-disabled client to the code that needs fresh reads.
L143: ## Pricing
L144: 
L145: ### Does Hyperdrive charge for data transfer / egress?
L146: 
L147: No.
L148: 
L149: ### Is Hyperdrive available on the cite69†Workers Free plan?
L150: 
L151: Yes. Refer to cite47†pricing .
L152: 
L153: ### Does Hyperdrive charge for additional compute?
L154: 
L155: Hyperdrive itself does not charge for compute (CPU) or processing (wall clock) time. Workers querying Hyperdrive and computing results: for example, serializing results into JSON and/or issuing queries, are billed per cite69†Workers pricing .
L156: 
L157: ## Limits
L158: ### Are there any limits to Hyperdrive?
L159: 
L160: Refer to the published cite48†limits documentation.

L95: # What are Durable Objects?
L96: 
L97: Last updated Jul 15, 2026|Copy as Markdown|cite62†View as Markdown |cite53†Agent setup L98: 
L99: [Select]
L100: 
L101: A Durable Object is a special kind of cite63†Cloudflare Worker which uniquely combines compute with storage. Like a Worker, a Durable Object is automatically provisioned geographically close to where it is first requested, starts up quickly when needed, and shuts down when idle. You can have millions of them around the world. However, unlike regular Workers:
L102:   * Each Durable Object has a globally-unique name, which allows you to send requests to a specific object from anywhere in the world. Thus, a Durable Object can be used to coordinate between multiple clients who need to work together.
L103:   * Each Durable Object has some durable storage attached. Since this storage lives together with the object, it is strongly consistent yet fast to access.
L104: 
L105: Therefore, Durable Objects enable stateful serverless applications.
L106: ## Durable Objects highlights
L107: 
L108: Durable Objects have properties that make them a great fit for distributed stateful scalable applications.
L109: 
L110: Serverless compute, zero infrastructure management
L111:   * Durable Objects are built on-top of the Workers runtime, so they support exactly the same code (JavaScript and WASM), and similar memory and CPU limits.
L112:   * Each Durable Object is cite64†implicitly created on first access . User applications are not concerned with their lifecycle, creating them or destroying them. Durable Objects migrate among healthy servers, and therefore applications never have to worry about managing them.
L113:   * Each Durable Object stays alive as long as requests are being processed, and remains alive for several seconds after being idle before hibernating, allowing applications to cite43†exploit in-memory caching while handling many consecutive requests and boosting their performance.
L114: Storage colocated with compute
L115: 
L116:   * Each Durable Object has its own cite16†durable, transactional, and strongly consistent storage (up to 10 GB^{cite65†1 }), persisted across requests, and accessible only within that object.
L117: 
L118: Single-threaded concurrency
L119:   * Each cite13†Durable Object instance has an identifier , either randomly-generated or user-generated, which allows you to globally address which Durable Object should handle a specific action or request.
L120:   * Durable Objects are single-threaded and cooperatively multi-tasked, just like code running in a web browser. For more details on how safety and correctness are achieved, refer to the blog post cite66†"Durable Objects: Easy, Fast, Correct — Choose three" ↗†blog.cloudflare.com .
L121: Elastic horizontal scaling across Cloudflare's global network
L122:   * Durable Objects can be spread around the world, and you can cite67†optionally influence where each instance should be located . Durable Objects are not yet available in every Cloudflare data center; refer to the cite68†where.durableobjects.live ↗†where.durableobjects.live project for live locations.
L123:   * Each Durable Object type (or cite12†"Namespace binding" in Cloudflare terms) corresponds to a JavaScript class implementing the actual logic. There is no hard limit on how many Durable Objects can be created for each namespace.
L124:   * Durable Objects scale elastically as your application creates millions of objects. There is no need for applications to manage infrastructure or plan ahead for capacity.
L125: ## Durable Objects features
L126: ### In-memory state
L127: 
L128: Each Durable Object has its own cite43†in-memory state . Applications can use this in-memory state to optimize the performance of their applications by keeping important information in-memory, thereby avoiding the need to access the durable storage at all.
L129: 
L130: Useful cases for in-memory state include batching and aggregating information before persisting it to storage, or for immediately rejecting/handling incoming requests meeting certain criteria, and more.
L131: In-memory state is reset when the Durable Object hibernates after being idle for some time. Therefore, it is important to persist any in-memory data to the durable storage if that data will be needed at a later time when the Durable Object receives another request.
L132: ### Storage API
L133: 
L134: The cite16†Durable Object Storage API allows Durable Objects to access fast, transactional, and strongly consistent storage. A Durable Object's attached storage is private to its unique instance and cannot be accessed by other objects.
L135: 
L136: There are two flavors of the storage API, a cite17†key-value (KV) API and an cite16†SQL API .
L137: When using the cite69†new SQLite in Durable Objects storage backend , you have access to both the APIs. However, if you use the previous storage backend you only have access to the key-value API.
L138: ### Alarms API
L139: 
L140: Durable Objects provide an cite18†Alarms API which allows you to schedule the Durable Object to be woken up at a time in the future. This is useful when you want to do certain work periodically, or at some specific point in time, without having to manually manage infrastructure such as job scheduling runners on your own.
L141: 
L142: You can combine Alarms with in-memory state and the durable storage API to build batch and aggregation applications such as queues, workflows, or advanced data pipelines.
L143: ### WebSockets
L144: 
L145: WebSockets are long-lived TCP connections that enable bi-directional, real-time communication between client and server. Because WebSocket sessions are long-lived, applications commonly use Durable Objects to accept either the client or server connection.
L146: Because Durable Objects provide a single-point-of-coordination between Cloudflare Workers, a single Durable Object instance can be used in parallel with WebSockets to coordinate between multiple clients, such as participants in a chat room or a multiplayer game.
L147: 
L148: Durable Objects support the cite70†WebSocket Standard API , as well as the cite71†WebSockets Hibernation API which extends the Web Standard WebSocket API to reduce costs by not incurring billing charges during periods of inactivity.
L149: ### RPC
L150: 
L151: Durable Objects support Workers cite72†Remote-Procedure-Call (RPC) which allows applications to use JavaScript-native methods and objects to communicate between Workers and Durable Objects.
L152:

L154: ## Actor programming model
L155: 
L156: Another way to describe and think about Durable Objects is through the lens of the cite73†Actor programming model ↗†en.wikipedia.org . There are several popular examples of the Actor model supported at the programming language level through runtimes or library frameworks, like cite74†Erlang ↗†www.erlang.org , cite75†Elixir ↗†elixir-lang.org , cite76†Akka ↗†akka.io , or cite77†Microsoft Orleans for .NET ↗†learn.microsoft.com .

content.text:
## Audit verdict

Skillplane can adopt Nucleus’s regional-cell pattern, but it should **route by workspace, not by user**.

Nucleus assigns each identity a home region and routes authentication through regional account hostnames. That works for its model, but Skillplane users can belong to several workspaces—and those workspaces may require different regions. Copying Nucleus directly would make cross-region membership, service credentials, and MCP OAuth unnecessarily difficult.

Recommended shape:

```text
Browser / MCP client
        │
        ▼
app.skillplane.dev / mcp.skillplane.dev
Global gateway + control plane
  - authentication and OAuth
  - workspace directory
  - memberships and credentials
        │
        ├── workspace A ──► India cell ──► regional Postgres + bucket
        ├── workspace B ──► US cell    ──► regional Postgres + bucket
        └── workspace C ──► EU cell    ──► regional Postgres + bucket
```

This is a multi-region, single-writer-per-workspace architecture. It improves placement, residency options, and blast-radius isolation; it is not active-active failover.

## Findings

1. **[P0] Nucleus’s user-home-region key is unsuitable for Skillplane.**

   Nucleus exposes regional account authorities and resolves identities to `insouth`, `useast`, or `euwest` ([account README](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/services/account/README.md:5), [regional client](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions-dev/authfn/client/src/regional-client.ts:16)). Skillplane OAuth access tokens are opaque and user-scoped, while the workspace is selected later ([token issuance](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/authfn-mcp-oauth/src/tokens.ts:80), [verification](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/authfn-mcp-oauth/src/verify.ts:27)). Workspace placement therefore has to be resolved after authentication.

2. **[P1] Skillplane is presently hardwired to one data plane.**

   Deployment explicitly documents one PostgreSQL database and one private R2 bucket ([deployment.md](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/docs/operations/deployment.md:3)). Runtime bindings and configuration accept one Hyperdrive and one object store ([config](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/config/src/index.ts:33)), and service construction creates one database-backed AuthFn/DataFn/domain stack per request ([services](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/api/src/services.ts:33)). Both public Workers currently bind the same Hyperdrive and bucket.

3. **[P1] The domain model is mostly shard-ready, but identity and tenancy are physically coupled to it.**

   Skills, versions, contexts, notes, reviews, analytics, and audit rows are consistently workspace-scoped. That is the strongest enabling property.

   The blockers are that workspaces, memberships, invitations, and service principals have foreign keys into AuthFn tables in the same database ([domain schema](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/db/src/schema/domain.ts:28)). Personal-workspace provisioning and permission checks also join directly against AuthFn users ([tenancy](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/api/src/tenancy.ts:36)). Those joins cannot cross regional databases.

4. **[P1] Credentials cannot select a regional endpoint before verification.**

   OAuth tokens contain no routing hint. Service keys require AuthFn verification followed by a service-principal lookup to discover their workspace ([service-principal authentication](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/api/src/service-principal-auth.ts:64)). Keep authentication global and route internally after verification.

5. **[P1] Deployment, migration, backup, and rollback assume one origin.**

   The renderer requires exactly one Hyperdrive and the fixed `skillplane-skill-bundles` bucket ([render-deploy-config.mjs](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/scripts/render-deploy-config.mjs:26)). These procedures need per-cell manifests, backups, migrations, smoke checks, and rollback state before adding a second database.

6. **[P1] Do not copy Nucleus’s public identifier-to-region lookup.**

   The underlying lookup can return `userId`, region, and authority for an email ([regions.ts](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions-dev/authfn/core/src/core/regions.ts:113)). Skillplane deliberately preserves non-enumerating email behavior ([verify page](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/app/src/routes/verify/+page.svelte:260)). A stable global authentication origin avoids this privacy regression.

7. **[P2] Nucleus is a useful architectural reference, not production proof.**

   Its committed design already contains regional Workers, placement hints, per-region Hyperdrive, lookup storage, and generated Wrangler environments. However, current pre/live Hyperdrive values remain placeholders ([environments.json](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/services/account/config/environments.json:117)), and its checkout has extensive uncommitted work. Treat it as a pattern library rather than a deployable template.

## Recommended ownership split

| Global control plane | Regional workspace cell |
|---|---|
| AuthFn users, sessions and OTP | Skills and skill versions/files |
| OAuth clients, codes, access and refresh tokens | Contexts, knowledge and notes |
| Workspace ID, globally unique slug, region, state and routing epoch | Amendment reviews |
| Memberships, roles and invitations | Workspace-scoped idempotency |
| Service principals and API-key validation | Domain audit and analytics |
| `workspaces_list` and provisioning state | Regional object storage |
| Security/global audit events | Minimal workspace marker, not user records |

The control-plane directory should contain at least:

```text
workspace_id
slug
region_id
state: provisioning | active | migrating | suspended
routing_epoch
created_at
updated_at
```

Use central PostgreSQL uniqueness for slug reservation and route changes. A Durable Object can later serialize provisioning or migration operations, but it is not required merely because Nucleus uses one; central PostgreSQL already provides the authoritative transaction boundary. If introduced, Durable Objects provide strongly consistent, single-threaded coordination—not a replacement for the directory’s queryable source of truth. [Cloudflare Durable Objects documentation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/concepts/what-are-durable-objects/)

## Regional request flow

1. Authenticate the browser session, OAuth bearer token, or `spk_` key centrally.
2. Resolve and authorize the workspace centrally.
3. Read `workspace_id → region_id, routing_epoch`.
4. Produce a short-lived signed internal assertion containing actor, workspace, role/scopes, request ID, region, epoch, and expiry.
5. Forward the request to the appropriate private cell Worker.
6. The cell verifies the assertion and routing epoch before any side effect.

Use Cloudflare HTTP Service Binding `fetch()` calls. Regional cells should have no public route. Service bindings support private Worker-to-Worker forwarding, and the target Worker must be deployed before its caller. [Cloudflare Service Bindings documentation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/service-bindings/)

Use fetch handlers rather than RPC entrypoints for cells, because Worker placement applies to fetch execution; Cloudflare explicitly notes that Smart Placement does not affect RPC or named entrypoints. Each cell should use targeted placement near its PostgreSQL primary. [Cloudflare Placement documentation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/placement/)

A cell receiving stale routing should return `409 WORKSPACE_REGION_MISMATCH`. The gateway may invalidate its directory cache and retry once, but only if rejection happened before a side effect and the original idempotency key is preserved.

## Phased implementation

1. **Define the contract and region inventory.**

   Add a single configuration source analogous to Nucleus’s `environments.json`, describing region ID, Worker name, placement region, Hyperdrive, bucket, jurisdiction, enabled environments, and routing binding name.

2. **Split control-plane and data-plane interfaces while retaining one physical database.**

   Introduce `ControlPlaneServices` and `RegionalDataPlaneProvider`. Move authentication, directory, membership, invitations, and service-principal operations behind the control interface. Initially both providers can use today’s connection, preserving behavior.

3. **Turn today’s deployment into the default cell.**

   Keep all existing workspaces mapped to a default region. Extract a private regional cell Worker and make the app/MCP Workers route to it through service bindings. This proves the gateway boundary without moving any data.

4. **Remove cross-database constraints.**

   Replace regional AuthFn foreign keys with logical actor IDs. Move authoritative membership and service-principal records global. Regional tables receive a minimal workspace marker and trust only signed gateway authorization.

5. **Add a second cell for new workspaces.**

   Provision a second PostgreSQL/Hyperdrive pair and bucket. Initially place only newly created workspaces there. Organization workspaces should get an explicit region choice; personal workspaces can use a geography-derived default with an override.

6. **Build workspace migration tooling.**

   A safe migration is: quiesce writes, export workspace rows, copy referenced objects, verify counts and content digests, increment `routing_epoch`, atomically switch the directory, then retain the source copy for a rollback window. Avoid dual-write as the first migration mechanism.

7. **Operationalize additional regions.**

   Deploy cells before gateways, maintain N/N-1 internal API compatibility, run migrations and backups independently per cell, and publish per-cell health/SLO dashboards.

## Required validation

Before calling the second region production-ready, the test environment should use one control database, two regional databases, and two isolated object stores. It must cover:

- One user accessing workspaces in both regions.
- Global workspace-slug uniqueness.
- No cross-cell content leakage.
- OAuth and service-key access across cells.
- Stale directory cache and routing-epoch refresh.
- Duplicate/partial workspace provisioning.
- Wrong-region rejection before side effects.
- Idempotent retry behavior.
- Regional outage versus control-directory outage.
- Public retrieval and asset-download routing.
- Per-region migration, backup, rollback, and digest verification.

Keep Hyperdrive query caching disabled for auth, permissions, directory routing, and read-after-write paths; Cloudflare does not invalidate cached reads automatically after application writes. A second cache-enabled binding could later serve explicitly stale-tolerant public reads. [Cloudflare Hyperdrive FAQ](https://developers.cloudflare.com/hyperdrive/reference/faq/)

## Residency constraint

Separate buckets are useful for cell isolation, but an R2 `apac` location hint is only best-effort. R2 currently guarantees jurisdictional storage for EU, US, and FedRAMP—not India specifically. If India-local residency is a hard requirement, the cell needs an object-storage provider that contractually guarantees India rather than claiming an APAC hint satisfies it. [Cloudflare R2 data-location documentation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/reference/data-location/)

The first product decision should therefore be whether “multi-region” primarily means latency, blast-radius reduction, or legally guaranteed residency. If it is only latency, targeted placement against the current database is a much smaller first experiment. If it includes tenant placement or residency, the workspace-cell refactor above is the correct direction.

Audit scope: static read-only inspection of Skillplane at `3de2716`, Nucleus at `555cce7`, and current Cloudflare documentation. No files were changed, no tests were run, and no live Cloudflare, database, OAuth, or deployment state was mutated or treated as verified.

Workspace placement therefore has to be resolved after authentication.

2. **[P1] Skillplane is presently hardwired to one data plane.**

   Deployment explicitly documents one PostgreSQL database and one private R2 bucket ([deployment.md](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/docs/operations/deployment.md:3)). Runtime bindings and configuration accept one Hyperdrive and one object store ([config](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/config/src/index.ts:33)), and service construction creates one database-backed AuthFn/DataFn/domain stack per request ([services](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/api/src/services.ts:33)). Both public Workers currently bind the same Hyperdrive and bucket.

   Skills, versions, contexts, notes, reviews, analytics, and audit rows are consistently workspace-scoped. That is the strongest enabling property.

Personal-workspace provisioning and permission checks also join directly against AuthFn users ([tenancy](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/api/src/tenancy.ts:36)). Those joins cannot cross regional databases.

4. **[P1] Credentials cannot select a regional endpoint before verification.**

   OAuth tokens contain no routing hint. Service keys require AuthFn verification followed by a service-principal lookup to discover their workspace ([service-principal authentication](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/packages/api/src/service-principal-auth.ts:64)). Keep authentication global and route internally after verification.

5. **[P1] Deployment, migration, backup, and rollback assume one origin.**

   The renderer requires exactly one Hyperdrive and the fixed `skillplane-skill-bundles` bucket ([render-deploy-config.mjs](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/skillplane/scripts/render-deploy-config.mjs:26)).    The underlying lookup can return `userId`, region, and authority for an email ([regions.ts](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions-dev/authfn/core/src/core/regions.ts:113)). ## Recommended ownership split

| Global control plane | Regional workspace cell |
|---|---|
| AuthFn users, sessions and OTP | Skills and skill versions/files |
| OAuth clients, codes, access and refresh tokens | Contexts, knowledge and notes |
| Workspace ID, globally unique slug, region, state and routing epoch | Amendment reviews |
| Memberships, roles and invitations | Workspace-scoped idempotency |
| Service principals and API-key validation | Domain audit and analytics |
| `workspaces_list` and provisioning state | Regional object storage |
| Security/global audit events | Minimal workspace marker, not user records |

The control-plane directory should contain at least:

```text
workspace_id
slug
region_id
state: provisioning | active | migrating | suspended
routing_epoch
created_at
updated_at
```

Use central PostgreSQL uniqueness for slug reservation and route changes. A Durable Object can later serialize provisioning or migration operations, but it is not required merely because Nucleus uses one; central PostgreSQL already provides the authoritative transaction boundary. If introduced, Durable Objects provide strongly consistent, single-threaded coordination—not a replacement for the directory’s queryable source of truth. [Cloudflare Durable Objects documentation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/concepts/what-are-durable-objects/)

## Regional request flow

1. Authenticate the browser session, OAuth bearer token, or `spk_` key centrally.
2. Resolve and authorize the workspace centrally.
3. Read `workspace_id → region_id, routing_epoch`.
4. Produce a short-lived signed internal assertion containing actor, workspace, role/scopes, request ID, region, epoch, and expiry.
5. Forward the request to the appropriate private cell Worker.
6. The cell verifies the assertion and routing epoch before any side effect.

Use Cloudflare HTTP Service Binding `fetch()` calls. Regional cells should have no public route. Service bindings support private Worker-to-Worker forwarding, and the target Worker must be deployed before its caller. [Cloudflare Service Bindings documentation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/service-bindings/)

Use fetch handlers rather than RPC entrypoints for cells, because Worker placement applies to fetch execution; Cloudflare explicitly notes that Smart Placement does not affect RPC or named entrypoints. Each cell should use targeted placement near its PostgreSQL primary. [Cloudflare Placement documentation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/placement/)

A cell receiving stale routing should return `409 WORKSPACE_REGION_MISMATCH`. The gateway may invalidate its directory cache and retry once, but only if rejection happened before a side effect and the original idempotency key is preserved.

## Phased implementation

1. **Define the contract and region inventory.**

   Add a single configuration source analogous to Nucleus’s `environments.json`, describing region ID, Worker name, placement region, Hyperdrive, bucket, jurisdiction, enabled environments, and routing binding name.

2. **Split control-plane and data-plane interfaces while retaining one physical database.**

   Introduce `ControlPlaneServices` and `RegionalDataPlaneProvider`. Move authentication, directory, membership, invitations, and service-principal operations behind the control interface. Initially both providers can use today’s connection, preserving behavior.

3. **Turn today’s deployment into the default cell.**

   Keep all existing workspaces mapped to a default region. Extract a private regional cell Worker and make the app/MCP Workers route to it through service bindings. This proves the gateway boundary without moving any data.

4. **Remove cross-database constraints.**

   Replace regional AuthFn foreign keys with logical actor IDs. Move authoritative membership and service-principal records global. Regional tables receive a minimal workspace marker and trust only signed gateway authorization.

5. **Add a second cell for new workspaces.**

   Provision a second PostgreSQL/Hyperdrive pair and bucket. Initially place only newly created workspaces there. Organization workspaces should get an explicit region choice; personal workspaces can use a geography-derived default with an override.

6. **Build workspace migration tooling.**

   A safe migration is: quiesce writes, export workspace rows, copy referenced objects, verify counts and content digests, increment `routing_epoch`, atomically switch the directory, then retain the source copy for a rollback window. Avoid dual-write as the first migration mechanism.

7. **Operationalize additional regions.**

   Deploy cells before gateways, maintain N/N-1 internal API compatibility, run migrations and backups independently per cell, and publish per-cell health/SLO dashboards.

## Required validation

Before calling the second region production-ready, the test environment should use one control database, two regional databases, and two isolated object stores. It must cover:

- One user accessing workspaces in both regions.
- Global workspace-slug uniqueness.
- No cross-cell content leakage.
- OAuth and service-key access across cells.
- Stale directory cache and routing-epoch refresh.
- Duplicate/partial workspace provisioning.
- Wrong-region rejection before side effects.
- Idempotent retry behavior.
- Regional outage versus control-directory outage.
- Public retrieval and asset-download routing.
- Per-region migration, backup, rollback, and digest verification.

Keep Hyperdrive query caching disabled for auth, permissions, directory routing, and read-after-write paths; Cloudflare does not invalidate cached reads automatically after application writes. A second cache-enabled binding could later serve explicitly stale-tolerant public reads. [Cloudflare Hyperdrive FAQ](https://developers.cloudflare.com/hyperdrive/reference/faq/)

## Residency constraint

Separate buckets are useful for cell isolation, but an R2 `apac` location hint is only best-effort. R2 currently guarantees jurisdictional storage for EU, US, and FedRAMP—not India specifically. If India-local residency is a hard requirement, the cell needs an object-storage provider that contractually guarantees India rather than claiming an APAC hint satisfies it. [Cloudflare R2 data-location documentation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/reference/data-location/)

The first product decision should therefore be whether “multi-region” primarily means latency, blast-radius reduction, or legally guaranteed residency. If it is only latency, targeted placement against the current database is a much smaller first experiment. If it includes tenant placement or residency, the workspace-cell refactor above is the correct direction.
